_about: The module layer (ARCHITECTURE §2.2). A module is ONE durable capability — the only object the selector reasons about — and it is the join between the four curricula that previously floated apart: the 40-unit ladder (units), the 44-competency grammar grid (competency_codes), the TCF exam model (exam_tasks) and the resource toolbox (resources). Every ladder unit belongs to exactly one module, so the ladder becomes the first traversal of the module graph rather than a parallel curriculum. `skills` lists the ONLY skills a module is assessed in — the matrix is sparse by design (§3.5): ~26 modules x ~2 skills is ~55 cells, not 160, so each cell can accumulate enough observations to mean something. `requires` is ADVISORY (§2.4): a wrong prerequisite edge would deadlock the learner, so the selector may unlock a module whose competency_codes are already competent and log the override.

families.foundation: The machinery every later sentence is built from: sounds, core verbs, questions, negation, agreement.
families.functional: Getting something done in French: order, navigate, shop, deal with a service, invite.
families.comprehension: Understanding French that was not written for you — the skill TTS cannot train (§3 of the stress-test).
families.production: Saying and writing what you mean: narrate, describe, compare, explain, argue.
families.exam: The TCF task formats themselves, taken from the official structure rather than invented.

modules.name: Introduce yourself
modules.can_do: Give your name, where you're from, where you live, who your family is.

modules.name: Numbers, time and dates
modules.can_do: Count, tell the time, say the day — and catch them when someone else says them.

modules.name: The four verbs everything hangs on
modules.can_do: Use être, avoir, aller, faire and regular -er verbs in the present, with correct agreement.

modules.name: Ask a question
modules.can_do: Ask a question three ways, and ask someone to repeat or slow down — the sentence that rescues every real conversation.

modules.name: Say no
modules.can_do: Say what you don't do, don't have, don't understand.

modules.name: Describe your day
modules.can_do: Talk through a routine day, including pronominal verbs.

modules.name: Hold a first conversation
modules.can_do: Greet, introduce yourself, ask two questions, answer, and close — six turns without freezing.

modules.name: Order and pay
modules.can_do: Order a coffee, ask the price, pay — with a polite conditional rather than a bare imperative.

modules.name: Find your way
modules.can_do: Say where something is, ask for and follow directions, talk about how you get around.

modules.name: Buy things
modules.can_do: Shop for food: quantities, partitives, saying there isn't any.

modules.name: Handle an appointment or a call
modules.can_do: Book an appointment, say what hurts, leave a phone message, spell your name.

modules.name: Describe people and places
modules.can_do: Describe where you live and what someone looks like, with adjectives that agree.

modules.name: Invite, accept, refuse
modules.can_do: Invite someone, accept warmly, refuse politely and give a reason.

modules.name: Follow everyday French
modules.can_do: Follow a familiar exchange or a short announcement at natural speed — small talk, weather, how long you've been doing something.

modules.name: Follow a story
modules.can_do: Follow a narrative told by a native speaker: who did what, when, and what was already going on.

modules.name: Catch someone's position
modules.can_do: Hear an opinion and identify the position, the reasons behind it, and what the speaker concedes.

modules.name: Say what you like
modules.can_do: Say what you like and dislike doing, and how often.

modules.name: Say what happened
modules.can_do: Report what you did — including an incident at work — in the passé composé, with être/avoir chosen correctly.

modules.name: Talk about what's ahead
modules.can_do: Talk about plans and the future, informally and formally, including si + présent conditions.

modules.name: Describe how things used to be
modules.can_do: Use the imparfait for habits, background and what things were like.

modules.name: Tell a story
modules.can_do: Tell a story that holds together: events in the passé composé against a background in the imparfait, with agreement right.

modules.name: Stop repeating yourself
modules.can_do: Use le/la/les, lui/leur, y, en and qui/que/où so sentences join up instead of restarting.

modules.name: Compare two things
modules.can_do: Compare jobs, cities, seasons — more than, less than, the best.

modules.name: Give an opinion and back it up
modules.can_do: State a position, give two reasons and an example, explain cause and consequence, and answer a disagreement.

modules.name: Organise a longer answer
modules.can_do: Sequence and structure what you say: first, then, on the other hand, finally — so a two-minute answer has a shape.

modules.name: TCF writing task 1
modules.can_do: Write a 60–120 word message to someone you know: describe, invite, thank — on format and on time.

modules.name: TCF: ask for information
modules.can_do: Ask eight well-formed questions to enrol, rent or register — including indirect questions.
